newsitem.title: GERMANY: German life insurers urge company pensions boost.
newsitem.headline: German life insurers urge company pensions boost.

text.p: Germany urgently needs a framework and tax incentives to boost company pension schemes, leading life insurers insist.
Corporate schemes play a small and shrinking role just as pressure is mounting on state coffers and a demographic upheaval threatens to double Germany's over-65 population by 2030.
At a seminar late on Wednesday, Gerhard Rupprecht, chairman of market leader Allianz Lebensversicherungs AG, castigated Bonn for not promoting alternatives to state pensions.
"Looking back at the current legislative period, it is clear that the message got through, but the faith is lacking. Our legislators have not yet managed to set up any solutions," Rupprecht said.
"We have to make sure that investments are made outside the state system. We must find a tax system that actually promotes savings," he added.

Corporate schemes, always a minor player in German pension provision, have lost ground in recent years. In 1994, they accounted for just 13 percent of pension spending, compared with 17 percent for private pension schemes and the state's 70 percent share.

The decline comes amid a growing, and universally accepted, need to ease the pressure on state pension schemes, with experts predicting that thirty years from now, over 40 percent of Germans will be pensioners.

Supported by the German Life Insurers' Association, Rupprecht said a key solution would be to remove disincentives such as the double tax that currently applies to pensions -- one tax on contributions and another on benefit payments.
In addition, companies and employees need to be presented with more attractive models to the current pension schemes on offer, he said.

Rupprecht proposed a system of outside funding for corporate pensions, in which a pension fund, called a Euro-Pensionskasse and subject to life insurance industry supervision, would take over the running of the scheme.
The scheme would free firms from having to make expensive provisions for pension payouts and benefit savers by removing the risk of corporate insolvency from their funds, he said.

Brushing aside suggestions that a separate pensions regulator would be needed, to offset such disasters as the Robert Maxwell fiasco in Britain, Rupprecht said Germany's existing life insurance supervision authority would suffice.

Assets would be managed "German-style", which translates into a highly conservative approach to risk and a strong weighting toward fixed-income investments, a sharp contrast to the typical Anglo-Saxon pension fund with its clear bias toward equity holdings.

In a statement released to coincide with the seminar, the Life Insurers' Association urged further efforts to improve liquidity on the German equity market, which it said was partly to blame for life insurers' reluctance to invest in stocks.
Rupprecht added that the launch of the Euro, planned for 1999, should help to facilitate more equity investments, as this would remove the "considerable currency risk we now face in Europe."
"The tendency (for more share investment) will be quite clear in the time ahead," Rupprecht said.
